entry.title: Tom Skerritt, ‘Alien’ and ‘M*A*S*H’ Star, Dies at 93
entry.summary: Tom Skerritt, whose acting career spanned seven decades and played Dallas in "Alien" and Duke in "M*A*S*H," has died. He was 93.
entry.content:
Tom Skerritt, the American screen actor who was first billed in Ridley Scott’s horror classic “Alien” (1979) and sustained a career spanning more than seven decades, died Wednesday of natural causes, according to media reports. He was 93.

Skerritt first rose to prominence with a breakout turn in Robert Altman’s Korean War comedy “M*A*S*H,” playing the surgeon Duke Forrest. He was third-billed in the feature, after then-more-established stars Donald Sutherland and Elliott Gould. The role launched him to a prolific Hollywood career that saw him garner more than 100 screen credits. He kept acting through the final years of his life, with his most recent project being a supporting role in the 2025 Western “Broke” starring Wyatt Russell.

More to come…

entry.title: Cinema Eye Honors Unveil Nominees for 2027’s Best Documentary Films and Series
entry.summary: 2027 Cinema Eye Honors reveal its Audience Choice Prize Longlist, its Unforgettables Honorees, its Broadcast nominees, and its Shorts List.
entry.content:
The Cinema Eye Honors, one of the main bellwethers for the Best Documentary Feature race, began its 20th annual celebrations with a first wave of awards announcements for its 2027 ceremony.

17 films made it onto its Audience Choice Prize Longlist, including Sundance breakouts like “American Doctor” and “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” as well as recent box office successes “The History of Concrete” and “You Can See Everything.”

The organization’s Unforgettable Honorees, an award celebrating on-camera collaborators, were also announced with the 2027 winners coming from six films: Dr. Thaer Ahmad, Dr. Mark Perlmutter and Dr. Feroze Sidhwa from “American Doctor,” E. Jean Carroll from “Ask E. Jean,” Soraya Akhlaghi from “A Fox Under a Pink Moon,” Billie Jean King from “Give Me the Ball,” Israa from “One in a Million,” and Amy Goodman from “Steal This Story, Please!”

Related Stories
‘Moonlight’ Turns 10: Tarell Alvin McCraney on the Film’s Lasting Legacy and That Best Picture Mix-Up
Artists Equity’s Amy Baer on Building a Sustainable Indie Model with Movies That Don’t Star Matt Damon or Ben Affleck

On the Broadcast side, nominees were announced for five different categories, from Outstanding Achievement in Broadcast Film to Outstanding Achievement in Broadcast Editing. The annual Shorts List, spotlighting 10 of the year’s top documentary short films, including “They’re Here” co-directed by Oscar winner Laura Poitras, was also part of the announcement.

Finally, “Hoop Dreams,” Steve James’ documentary masterpiece, will receive the Legacy Award, which is presented to a classic nonfiction film that continues to inspire today’s working filmmakers. James will accept the award on behalf of his team members Peter Gilbert (Producer and DP), Frederick Marx (Producer and Editor), Adam Singer (Sound Recordist), Gordon Quinn (Executive Producer and founder of Kartemquin Films), Bill Haugse (Editor), Marcie McCall (Kartemquin) and Ben Sidran (Composer).

Cinema Eye will celebrate its 20th annual Awards Ceremony on Monday, January 11, 2027.

entry.title: ‘Moonlight’ Turns 10: Tarell Alvin McCraney on the Film’s Lasting Legacy and That Best Picture Mix-Up
entry.summary: Oscar-winning screenwriter Tarell Alvin McCraney reflects on the beginnings of 'Moonlight,' to he and director Barry Jenkins winning an Academy Award.
entry.content:
The word playwright and screenwriter Tarell Alvin McCraney uses to describe his thoughts on the journey his deeply personal film “Moonlight” continues to have is “incredible.” Wednesday, October 21, marks 10 years since the Best Picture Oscar winner was released to the masses. ”Seeing it now is worth the price of admission,” said the Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar winner to IndieWire over Zoom.

An adaptation of his unproduced play “In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue,” written with director Barry Jenkins, “Moonlight” still has McCraney asking himself the fundamental question, “‘Who am I and who can I be?’ And that’s powerful.”

Related Stories
Artists Equity’s Amy Baer on Building a Sustainable Indie Model with Movies That Don’t Star Matt Damon or Ben Affleck
Don’t Get the Wrong Idea About ‘The Dropout’

The current Geffen Playhouse artistic director, who is still working on many TV and film projects he is not yet allowed to discuss, said, “I’m still expanding like the universe. And the moment that I stop, the moment that I just sit in it, then where am I?”

Read on for more of McCraney reflecting on “Moonlight” at 10 below.

How “Moonlight” Came to Be

“So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was a film, a screenplay that I wrote in 2003, right after the death of my mother. She died of AIDS-related complications. And I had written a play called ‘The Brothers Size’ for my entry into the Yale School of Drama and the script called ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue.’ I had written both of them because, one, I was making an application for grad school, but two, my teacher, Rafael Lima, who was our playwriting and screenplay teacher in high school, always told me that if a story was coming to you visually, then it’s a film. If you heard it, it was a play. So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was always slated to be a film because it was coming to me in images, but I’d written it in a kind of hybrid, what I call a medium length.

“It wasn’t a full feature at the time. I previously had written a short in high school called ‘Silent Type,’ and it was more about me trying to put down the memories I was having of growing up in Liberty City. Now, I understand it’s something most people do when losing a parent. They sort of start trying to recollect their earliest memories and put them back together again. So that’s how ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ came about. But in 2003, an indie film about a gay kid in Miami was probably a hard feat, especially for a just-recently-graduated undergrad. So André Holland, who I met later, had read a copy of it, Glenn Davis, who runs Steppenwolf, we had all read a copy and tried to make it into a film in Chicago. Then I quickly sort of said, ‘No, this is where we stay.’ And it stayed in my computer for probably another 10 years until I met Barry Jenkins in around 2012, 2013.

“We were both making a film in a film festival here in Miami. We had a couple meetings, and found out we grew up blocks away from each other. Barry said, ‘Look, I want to make this into a film. I’ve read the script.’ Our friend Andrew Hevia had given it to him. He said, ‘I think I can make this into a full feature.’ I was like, ‘Great, we should.’ He didn’t believe me a few times. This is before there was an A24 or Plan B involved. So I think he thought I didn’t believe him. He kept going back, getting more support, and saying, ‘Look, we’re going to make this into a film.’ I kept going, ‘Yes, yes you are.’

“So even to this day, he said, ‘Yeah, you did have to say yes to me a few times before I believed you.’ But yeah, that’s how we came together on the film. Barry did an incredible job of turning it into a full feature, taking the story that was already there and taking it from a place of memory into a place of palpability and something that we all could feel.”

On the Role YoungArts Played in “Moonlight” Being Made

“I have had an incredible education in art thanks to Miami. Miami’s art has been nurtured in a real way by YoungArts and The National Foundation for the Advancement of the Arts, specifically young artists, because it brings in artists from all over the world.

“I remember sneaking out of playwriting class to go to YoungArts to see the YoungArts finalists and thinking, ‘Those dancers are doing what I’m supposed to be doing in their form right now. Their dedication, their ability to control their body and use their technique is — ’ And I’m just over here in this acting class trying to remember my lines. I just thought even then, ‘I’ve got to get my shit together.’

“And so YoungArts has really paved a way for that. They have really dedicated themselves to nurturing the local artists, but also bringing in young artists and supporting them for longer stretches of time. That’s been so helpful. Andrew Hevia, who was an arts finalist, is the reason why Barry Jenkins and I met each other because he was producing films and said to us, ‘Hey, you both are Miami. You both have Miami connections. You should know each other.’

“YoungArts was instrumental in giving us space to do pre-production for ‘Moonlight.’ That organization has really carved a path for arts in this community in a way that national foundations rarely do. So I’m ever grateful for them and wish them nothing but success and hope that other national organizations, that the government, that our local folks really help celebrate them and keep them around for a long time.”

On How He Saw “Moonlight” for the First Time

“Watching it for the first time, even in New York, because though I was near and helping on production, I was not on set. There were just too many places that they were going to that were places I had grown up and places that I had actually lived in. So I didn’t know how I would feel sitting on a set in those moments. But I do remember watching a great deal of those moments on film, in screening rooms, and it was beautiful. First I thought, ‘Wow, I’m so glad that this exists. I’m so glad that these memories have been immortalized in these ways with these incredible artists rendering it for all of us to see.’

“Seeing it at TIFF, something else happened, which was like, ‘Oh, wow. And now I’m sharing all of these things with 2,200 people.’ And I did not expect that. I will tell you, and I’ve said to many people, whether people think it’s naïve or shortsighted, I really thought, ‘Yeah, a few hundred thousand people may see this film in total.’ I grew up on indie films. I grew up in Miami going to places like O Cinema, and my mentor would take us to art films all the time here in the cinema. So it was something that we were used to even when the blockbusters like ‘Bad Boys’ were being made here, we were still watching ‘Before Night Falls.’

“So I was used to that and thought, ‘This is going to be a great addition to that.’ It blew my mind to see that it was going beyond that, that it was pushing past that, that this was going to be seen by maybe millions of people. I don’t know that I’ve still come to full terms with that. It’s the reason why I look shocked and surprised when people want to talk to me about the film even now.”

On Mahershala Ali’s Oscar-Winning Performance as Juan in “Moonlight”

“Mahershala and I crossed paths prior to ‘Moonlight’ because he was supposed to be in my play ‘In the Red and Brown Water.’ He is an incredible actor and was on stage then, and we were trying to get him into this play, and he sent me this note saying he’s so sorry he had to go do this other play and we couldn’t do it. So we ended up not working together on that, but I admired his work and loved seeing him on stage and on television as well. At the time, he was filming two or three shows.

“So when it came to the moment where Barry said, ‘Hey, here’s who we’re going to for Juan,’ I said, ‘Yeah, that’ll do.’ I always felt like it made sense, and the character clearly is based on someone who made a deep influence on my life as a young person. So there was no doubt in my mind that Mahershala would be extraordinary.”

On Naomie Harris’ Oscar-Nominated Performance as Paula in “Moonlight”

“It was incredible. She had about three or four days on set to film all of that. I didn’t know Naomie before, but she is an incredible artist who came in and just went, and it was extraordinary to watch. Sometimes it was hard to watch because she just went to this place where — that character couldn’t be more not like her. And especially in the earlier moments where she really embodies a lot of what my mother stood for, and then in the decline that she has in the film, some of the terror that my mother was going through. Thankfully, Barry kept the reconciliation that happens in the film that was in the script. He kept that and actually built on it in a way that was really gorgeous and really beautiful. So I was ever grateful for her portrayal, for going there, because she could have played it safe and she didn’t.”

On the Visual Legacy of “Moonlight”

“At the time, when we were both making and premiering the film, the democratizing, or the ability for folks to make film or visual depictions has exploded. In fact, the next film that I did make was shot on an iPhone. So the ability for people to make visual depictions and reach towards cinematic success became more palpable or more accessible. There were a lot of folks who were going, ‘Well, if those folks can do that, I can do this.’ And that was really extraordinary. I had tons of people write and say, ‘This made me go to film school. This made me take up cinematography in a way. This made me become a photographer.’ Literally, I have so many friends who just went, ‘Yeah, I write, but now I’m also a photographer, and I take it seriously, and I’m really about visual lenses.’ So that’s been extraordinary.

“That impact, a lot of it for me was being able to say, ‘Hey, I needed to make this film because I needed to see myself, or at least parts of myself that I wasn’t seeing.’ And I think a lot of folks went, ‘Yeah, I need to do the same.’ And I am grateful for that. And that happens: Films come along and do that. Films come along, or songs come along, or something happens in art where people go, ‘Oh, that artist really needed to see that depiction of themselves. I feel that, too, and want to do the same.’ So again, it was a gift to me that it is happening for other folks.

“When you think of a depiction of Black folk, specifically Black queer folks, there is a level of intimacy that the film has that folks recognized as ‘Oh wow, you can get that vulnerable on a subject that isn’t often seen.’ And again, when I say vulnerable, I mean the closeness of the shots, the deep peering into eyes that we hadn’t seen before. We’ve done that on tons of film. If you go back and look at some of the noir, you can get tons of close-ups of X, Y, and Z, but you watch things like ‘Ordinary People,’ and you see just how close and intimate, into the heat, that the camera gets. There are, of course, examples of those rituals like the baptism that happens to Chiron/Little by Juan, but they’re fewer and far between. The film is saying, ‘Hey, you can get closer to this and do more of it.’ And there’s a lot of filmmakers who have found their ideology, their way in through that, and found their own unique stamp to put on it, which is extraordinary.”

On “Moonlight” Entering the Best Adapted Screenplay Category — Even Though the Play Was Never Produced

“‘Fences’ is a play and then was adapted into a film, and so Adapted made sense. Again, you take a short, and you turn it into a feature length, and that’s an adaptation too. So it felt right to be there, for sure. Barry did really make it into a feature.

“The original script told this story in a very circular way, meaning you woke up and you realized that you would see the day going on of Little, Chiron, and Black all at once. So you would see one wake up, wash their face, the other get up, wash their face. At some point you realized that this was one life that you were watching. Barry thought, ‘No, we can chapter this out and make this more linear.’

“And then, he, of course, blew up that last 20 to 30 minutes of the film. [It] is an incredible Barry Jenkins lean-in, but peppering tons of shit that I do in my own life. I was like, ‘How did you…’ So yeah, adaptation, absolutely. It was incredible to collaborate with him on that, and I wish we could do it more.”

On Whether “Moonlight” Is Too Enmeshed with the Best Picture Mix-Up with “La La Land”

“It’s one of those things that just is. It’s like in the story, Juan disappears out of Little’s life, and it is just one of those things that is.

“And I don’t think that has tarnished the film in any way. The film is still the film. But yeah, it happened, and I’m grateful for however it manifested. I can’t undo it.

“I remember saying this to my friend Jeremy Pope — not just talking about this, but just life in general — I said, ‘Jay, if you don’t count it all joy, then you won’t stop counting.’ You have to count it all as joy. Every time you have to count it all joy, and it feels like one of those counts. You just count it all joy that we are headed towards this direction, that we’re 10 years out, and that this film that a lot of wonderful people put a lot of incredible work into was recognized in many ways.”

entry.title: ‘The Hunger Games’ Producer Nina Jacobson Talks Using AI to Test ADR Lines Before Recording with Actors: ‘We Would Never Use It’ in the Film
entry.summary: "Hunger Games" franchise producer Nina Jacobson explains AI's place in the post-production process and why the series resonates in Trump's America.
entry.content:
AI is continuing to be implemented in the post-production stages of studio films, though “Hunger Games” franchise producer Nina Jacobson still views it as a “tool for artists” and “not a substitute” for them.

During a conversation with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang at IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles Jacobson said the team used AI approximations of actors to test out new line readings for the upcoming prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Those lines would then be recorded with the cast in traditional automated dialogue replacement process.

“We just finished [post-production], fairly recently, on ‘Sunrise on the Reaping.’ We used [AI] very specifically as a tool — within production, within post-production — while, at the same time, never using it to ever replace any of our artists or anything you see onscreen,” Jacobson said. “When you have ADR you want try out, you used to either have the editor getting in there with the lines you wanted … Just for something you’re trying out that you might not even keep. [AI] is a great tool to use ADR.”

Related Stories
Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently
WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’

Jacobson went on to explain how the technology has relatively limited applications for her, none of which find their way onto the screen.

“They can duplicate a voice. You can have the thing that you want to go get, or do a slug that actually looks like what you want … But we would still never use it because it’s not our actors,” she continued. “We’d go to our writer for the dialogue. I don’t ask Claude, ‘What should they say?’ I don’t ask Claude to finish the movie for us. But as a tool within production [and] within post-production that advances your work, and ultimately gets you to a better creative outcome, it’s crazy not to make use of the tool that the entire world now seems to be hinging upon.”

The prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” in theaters from Lionsgate on November 20, is the sixth film adaptation of Suzanne Collins’ popular young adult books series. The movie franchise first launched in 2012, with three additional entries produced quickly in the immediate years. Lionsgate revived the property in 2023 with the prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” exploring the early politicking of the dystopian world of Panem and how the tyrant President Snow came to power.

“We don’t make the movies unless [Collins] writes a book. We’re not trying to just milk this title,” Jacobson said when asked about the franchise’s longevity. “They speak so much to the way that we live now and how we are living. The last one was really about the allure of authoritarianism. Why do we embrace it as a political system? Why are people drawn to it? … This one is about resistance: the cost of [it, and] the fact that just because something is a certain way today does not mean it always will be. You cannot predict the future based on the status quo.”

“Young people are growing up at a time where it seems impossible that we would ever be able to address climate change or the recession in democracy that we’ve seen across the globe, and yet it is that propaganda that kind of keeps you in that place of believing there’s nothing I can do to make a difference,” Jacobson continued. “Sometimes you won’t see the consequences of your resistance [in] four years, or maybe even in your lifetime. But it still adds up. … Whether you’ve seen none of the movies or all of them, it feels very much like a movie about the times we live in.”

Along with Jacobson’s “Hunger Games” talk, the producer touched on other projects from her film production company Color Force, including the coming “Dirty Dancing” sequel starring Jennifer Grey and HBO’s “Crazy Rich Asians” series. IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit also included a keynote by directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, diving into the production of their sci-fi blockbuster “Project Hail Mary,” and a one-on-one with Bill Hader on what he learned making his upcoming feature debut “They Know.”

Watch the complete conversation with Jacobson in the video above.

entry.title: Artists Equity’s Amy Baer on Building a Sustainable Indie Model with Movies That Don’t Star Matt Damon or Ben Affleck
entry.summary: Amy Baer of Matt Damon and Ben Affleck's Artists Equity talks to IndieWire about their new indie label and building a sustainable indie film model.
entry.content:
It can still be a struggle for people to grasp exactly what Ben Affleck and Matt Damon‘s Artists Equity banner is all about or how it works. In some cases it’s even hard for its own leaders to articulate what gives the company its secret sauce.

“I think they’re beginning to understand it, but I think that people don’t really understand the ambition and scope of this business,” Amy Baer, Artists Equity’s president of film and television and the No. 2 to Matt and Ben, told IndieWire.

“It is existing to enable and preserve the art of visual storytelling,” she continued. “[Damon and Affleck] are deeply, deeply rooted in the history of film. They are cinephiles, both of them, passionate cinephiles who not only want to redefine how creatives — both in front of the camera and behind the camera — are compensated, which is obviously the foundational component of our company, the equity piece, but to also ensure that we are creating a virtuous cycle so that it can endure.”

Related Stories
Don’t Get the Wrong Idea About ‘The Dropout’
‘The Debut’ Is the Go-to Festival Crowdpleaser as Jesse Eisenberg’s Musical Comedy Launches at Virginia

But Baer feels her job in explaining the Artists Equity model to people just got a little easier with the launch of the company’s new independent label, Artists Equity Independent Pictures (AEIP). The label, which will be led by former Topic Studios physical production exec Jennifer Westin as reporting to Baer, will use the same financial model that has allowed films like Artists Equity’s “Air,” “The Rip,” “Animals,” and “The Instigators” to get made. By asking talent to actually invest and take equity in the film, they take a smaller fee up front but can receive a better backend in the film’s success.

“That is the indie model, right? I spent 14 years as an independent producer. Everyone involved in every movie I made took less up front in order to help get the movie made,” Baer said. “In a typical indie film, 50 percent of the points go to the filmmaking team, the other 50 percent go to the financiers. We just say to the creative team, ‘Here’s your points. Carve it up.’ We’re not going to tell you how to do it.”

For an independent project under Artists Equity, that model can mean being able to secure a higher end editor, composer, or star who might not normally work for less. Baer views it as the same model that has served independent film for years, but with a few sweeteners in certain places.

The first project under the AEIP banner is “A Woman in the Sun,” which is written and directed by “Love of Your Life” and “Nyad” screenwriter Julia Cox and stars Renée Zellweger, Sissy Spacek, and Mia Threapleton. Black Bear is already set up as a distributor. Also just announced was Sam Jones’ “Downriver,” which will star Garrett Hedlund, Jake Lacy, and Jessica Biel.

Baer says the label is genre agnostic, but it’s not going for low budget slasher horror or experimental films, rather elevated, yet still commercial indie gems that have the potential to break out and have a clear audience in front of them.

AEIP is going to be searching for packaged projects rather than developing internally, then working with filmmakers to set an initial budget, and to identify emerging talent, be they first-time directors or fifth-timers. Baer says the worst thing this label can do is to spend money just because they have it, so things will be very judicious in the early days.

But the label was built on Damon and Affleck’s belief that there are a lot of movies that deserve a shot to get made but that shouldn’t have to rely on a 2000-screen commitment in order to even get financing. And having Matt and Ben championing those films doesn’t hurt.

“[The idea is] to really start to support the next generation of directors and writer-directors under an auspice that has the heft of being able to run the gauntlet on the marketing, distribution, promotion, and even in the packaging to a certain extent,” Baer said. “To have the two of them sitting atop the label gives a heft that I think is very unique to our company. There’s plenty of really good independent film companies out there, but I don’t think any of them have two Oscar winners sitting on top of it.”

One important distinction between AEIP movies and those under the flagship Artists Equity banner is that the indies won’t be bound by either of AE’s output deals, including Netflix for streaming and Sony Pictures for theatrical. Both of those deals require minimum budget levels that AEIP movies will typically be beneath. Netflix or Sony can still buy one if they love it.

Like those bigger budget projects though, AEIP movies will still qualify for performance bonuses if the film reaches certain viewership thresholds on streaming. That was the case with “The Rip,” in which Artists Equity paid out a percentage of the salary for each of the 1,200 crew members on the film. Baer didn’t disclose what those viewership thresholds were or how much individuals got paid in bonuses except to say it was “robust” views and a “substantial” bonus.

AEIP will need to be budget conscious and acutely aware of the audience for any of its films. “Kiss of the Spider Woman,” a musical remake starring Jennifer Lopez that premiered at Sundance, flopped hard with just $1.8 million at the box office against a $30 million budget. That movie predated Baer, but it’s a teaching moment all the same to be clear on what the market is telling you.

Baer reminds though that for all their star power today, Damon and Affleck have true indie roots, running around with Kevin Smith in the ’90s trying to get any shot they could. What she believes sets Artists Equity apart from the likes of MRC, Fifth Season, or even A24 is that they’re a company led by two A-listers who take the CEO and chief creative officer role as seriously as they do acting, writing, or directing.

“I think people really underestimate the ambition of the company. This is not a talent production company on steroids,” Baer said. “They both take that job incredibly seriously and are committed to being as nimble and as forward-facing as possible to make sure that the thing they love doing the most endures.”

The one thing Baer says is not part of her mandate is finding projects for Matt and Ben, who need no help with that. So it’s pretty unlikely that Affleck or Damon would actually star in one of these indies themselves, but they won’t be far away.

“They’re very disciplined about where they’re going to spend their time and energy, and they don’t want to leverage it just for the sake of getting things made. They want to empower other people to get things made,” Baer said. “It’s something that other companies can’t necessarily offer because those guys will get attention when they decide that they’re going to go help promote one of our films. What’s been really evident is that they’re very disciplined about we’re not going to make this and do that supporting role just so that we can justify making it. They want these things to stand on their own two feet.”

entry.title: Don’t Get the Wrong Idea About ‘The Dropout’
entry.summary: Watching Elizabeth Holmes watch "The Dropout" may leave viewers questioning the merits of Amanda Seyfried's Emmy-winning limited series. It shouldn’t.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: The following article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”]

Among the snippets of “The Dropout” shown in “You Can See Everything,” Amanda Seyfried dancing to “I’m in a Hurry (And Don’t Know Why)” is by far my favorite.

The scene sees Seyfried portraying a 17-year-old Elizabeth Holmes as she stares intently at a poster of Steve Jobs, semi-rhythmically churning her arms and letting herself be seduced by the Apple inventor’s image. As she bends and sways to Alabama’s country-rock classic (in the first of many dance scenes scattered throughout “The Dropout”), it’s as if her ambition is trying to shake free from her body. Her focus shifts, from implicit personal frustrations to an idea sparked by her idol, but it never wavers. She’s determined. Driven. Her famously imposing peepers bulge with excitement.

Related Stories
‘The Debut’ Is the Go-to Festival Crowdpleaser as Jesse Eisenberg’s Musical Comedy Launches at Virginia
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon to Present Free ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ New York City Screenings

In the context of the film, the scene is ridiculous. On a computer screen in front of the real Holmes is an exaggerated version of the Theranos founder, who’s watching along with her husband, Billy Evans, and documentarian, Nathan Fielder. When Fielder asks, “Did you really do that?” the answer is a foregone conclusion: Of course she didn’t. And if she did, she would never admit to it now.

In the context of the show, the scene is also ridiculous. The exaggerated version of Holmes isn’t meant to be a reenactment, like what Fielder orchestrates with Seyfried later in the movie. It’s a character, used to illustrate fundamental truths about the elusive tech founder and convicted fraudster: She’s obsessed with changing the world, she can’t wait to get started, and — perhaps most importantly — she doesn’t know why.

Therein lies the merit, the distinction, the ingenuity of “The Dropout,” which some audiences may struggle to recognize in the immediate, mind-bending aftermath of “You Can See Everything.” Even Seyfried, who emerges in the doc’s second half as the voice of the people and the project’s most valuable performer, struggles to defend the show after watching Holmes watch it. When pressed about her portrayal, a visibly rattled Seyfried hides behind the simplest explanation: “The Dropout” is a fictionalized TV show, and she’s playing a character.

That’s true, it’s just not the whole truth. It’s understandable for an actor to be a bit thrown when confronting a reality she’d previously only been able to play out in her head. (Seyfried meeting Holmes’ children, presumably without their mother’s knowledge, is one of the movie’s squirmiest moments.) But the show only needs defending if you haven’t seen it; if your main impression is from the film — where it’s contained to a section enmeshed in Elizabeth’s perspective — and not from first-hand experience within Elizabeth Meriwether’s probing, measured, and gleefully entertaining miniseries.

The show’s take on Holmes depicts the facts to interrogate the person. The movie’s take on Holmes directly interrogates the person to try to uncover the facts. When taken together, the unambiguous character Seyfried plays in the series stands shoulder to shoulder with the very ambiguous character Holmes may or may not be playing in the documentary: unknowable, yet — no matter what you believe — still ridiculous.

Before going any further, a quick reminder: Comparison is the thief of joy. No one needs to believe “The Dropout” is better than “You Can See Everything” to recognize the artistic achievements in both. While it’s always tempting in our list-making, awards-crazed, oft-repetitive entertainment era to elevate one project by claiming its superiority over another, such facile contentions tend to provoke more than they stimulate. They’re also particularly silly when connecting two distinct mediums, like film and TV, which already face a cultural power imbalance. There are many forms of art, and art is subjective. So let’s not waste time fighting over which vision of Elizabeth Holmes is superior. Instead, let’s see what they tell us about Holmes, together.

“The Dropout” never pretends to understand everything about Holmes, and it has that in common with “You Can See Everything.” Despite the documentary’s fanatical quest to determine, as The Atlantic’s David Sims puts it, “whether Holmes is a master manipulator or someone so deeply convinced of her own genius that she can’t distinguish fiction from fact,” Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim end up reveling in her inscrutability as well. How we decide what we know about another person’s thoughts and feelings — what we really know — is up to the individual who’s deciding, and what the movie claims to know is decidedly, pointedly torn.

“The Dropout” is less ambiguous, but that doesn’t make it definitive. Yes, the show fictionalizes real events to tell a digestible, entertaining story. And yes, viewers will come away with the impression that Elizabeth Holmes lied her way to fame and fortune, over and over, knowingly and willfully. But the fraud depicted in “The Dropout” is based on the facts, and their role in Holmes’ story still matters. It matters quite a bit.

The Hulu series goes beyond recapping the ABC News reports that inspired it. It’s one of the rare biopics that refuses to reduce its subject’s motivations to a single transformative moment in their past, or place the blame on societal ills, or flatten her into an evil, unfeeling monster. It allows for the unknown, be it a rock that’s yet to be turned over or the grand ineffability of human nature. And while the documentary keeps its tight framing on the Holmes’ household, brilliantly replicating the bewitching immersion of spending time with “Liz,” “The Dropout” takes the same wide lens it gave Holmes and applies it to the sweeping consequences of her crimes.

There’s her fellow scientists, whose experienced voices point out the ethical lines Holmes’ crosses to get Theranos funded. (Stephen Fry is so well-cast — and so searingly heartbroken — as Ian Gibbons, the chief scientist Holmes betrays, fires, rehires, and betrays again.) There’s company executives she manipulates into buying in, motivated as much by the alleged altruism of her product as their own FOMO over the Silicon Valley tech boom. (Episode 4 is perfectly, almost pityingly titled “Old White Men.”) There’s the slew of professional sources Theranos intimidates and the college kids they go after in court, dozens of innocent people who come to represent the millions of people who were hurt, some irreparably, by Holmes’ company.

Holmes, of course, does not come off well here, but she shouldn’t. Actions speak louder than words, and her actions, as proven in court, are the show’s focus. “You Can See Everything” is less interested in what happened than why it happened. With their unprecedented access to Holmes, Fielder and Oppenheim aim to determine if their subject knew she was lying (and still is) or if she “just thinks differently,” to paraphrase Evans’ explanation.

Holmes is much easier to sympathize with if your impression is limited to her — her story, her life, and her family, which make up the bulk of the movie. So when the occasional person is asked if they’ve heard of Elizabeth Holmes and they simply cite “the Hulu show,” it’s easy to feel frustrated on her behalf. No one likes being spoken for, and Holmes had zero control over how she was depicted in “The Dropout.”

That points to a larger problem in our culture. Turning everything into entertainment, from the nightly news to people’s lives, makes us dumber. But it doesn’t mean the show itself is problematic. In a few years, people might respond to the same question (“Have you heard of Elizabeth Holmes?”) by saying they saw “the Nathan Fielder documentary.” Would that mean they’re more informed? More understanding? Does it bring them closer to the truth about Holmes, even when the documentary itself admits the closer we get, the less comprehensible she becomes?

Sometimes a healthy distance provides greater clarity, and while I wouldn’t say either project offers a definitive take on Holmes, that’s partly because neither claims it has. Both “The Dropout” and “You Can See Everything” ultimately contend that no matter what context you’re given — news reports, court documents, old interviews, books, TV shows, documentaries — Holmes remains a mystery.

Which brings us to the question of “characters.” In “You Can See Everything,” Holmes tries to get The New York Times to retract a statement attributed to her about Jennifer Lawrence potentially playing her in a movie: “They’re not playing me,” she said. “They’re playing a character I created.” The implication is Holmes would never admit to creating a character, because that would mean she was conscious of creating a character from the beginning — of putting on a persona to get what she wants. But if she’d done that, then she’d be admitting to knowingly deceiving people, which she can’t admit, since it would be tantamount to acknowledging fraud.

When exposed to her persona — the voice, the black turtleneck, the photo of her holding the tiny vial of blood (which she supposedly hates) — it’s hard to believe what you’re seeing is natural. But the alternative, that she’s been in character in front of every camera that’s ever been thrust in front of her, sounds equally impossible.

“The Dropout” lives in the first belief. It invites the incredulity sparked by Holmes’ bizarre persona through a heightened tone and within Seyfried’s all-in performance. You see her construct the character she’s going to play for the world because you need to see it in order to believe anyone else would believe in this woman and invest in her company. The series lets the facts of what happened provide whatever answers there are regarding Holmes’ inner truth, while using Seyfried’s character as a sometimes legible, sometimes illegible cypher.

“You Can See Everything” is more open to the second belief, or at least starts there, by holding some sympathy for the “real” Holmes. Fielder and Oppenheim don’t set out to make fun of a woman who’s been endlessly mocked for the past decade-plus, and the longer you sit with her, the more possible it feels that she’s been misrepresented and misunderstood all along.

Fielder’s genuine care and consideration extends so much that the film’s final third interrogates if he’s gone too far and can’t see her clearly anymore. After getting as close to her as possible, Fielder still may only be seeing what she wants him to see: the character. Holmes wants him to believe there is no character, that this is just who she is, but he can’t do that. He doesn’t know.

So what does he do? He asks Seyfried for help. He needs a little distance from his subject. He needs to see Holmes from a separate, studied, but still intimate perspective. He needs to see her as Seyfried did in “The Dropout.” It’s helpful, even if it initially seemed like an impediment.

Back in the beach house, when Holmes takes in the scene from “The Dropout” where Seyfried screams “I get the fucking money!” over and over, like a distinctly American wind-up toy, the real Holmes retreats from the screen and cries into pillow. Fielder sits awkwardly at the foot of the bed. Evans offers a reassuring hand. But even in this unmistakably human moment, her motivations are a mystery. Maybe she’s courting sympathy. Maybe she’s genuinely appalled. Maybe she’s simply overwhelmed by competing truths: that she doesn’t see herself in Seyfried’s performance, and that so many other people do.

It made me wonder when Fielder sits down to show Holmes “The Dropout” in the first place, is he giving her space to distinguish the real her from her unwanted public image, as the scene suggests? To refute the “lies” that have defined her until now? To draw the line between the character and the human being?

Or is he forcing Holmes to confront how other people see her? How the world sees her? That, outside of her own unique understanding of reality, there’s another reality where she looks ridiculous, and no one knows why.

“The Dropout” is available on Hulu. “You Can See Everything” is in theaters now.

entry.title: ‘The Debut’ Is the Go-to Festival Crowdpleaser as Jesse Eisenberg’s Musical Comedy Launches at Virginia
entry.summary: 'The Debut' also just won Middleburg's Audience Award, but two hours away from the Virginia Film Festival in Charlottesville.
entry.content:
Another day, another film festival. I have been on quite the fall festival tour, starting back in Telluride over Labor Day Weekend, back to Los Angeles for a bit, then the sprawling New York Film Festival, then Middleburg in Virginia, and finally, a festival in another part of this large state, the University of Virginia’s 39-year-old Virginia Film Festival (Oct. 21-25).

This year’s VAFF program offers 100 films and a smattering of starry attendees, including Visionary Award winners Nathan Lane (“The Birdcage”) and Jessica Lange (“Long Day’s Journey Into Night”), interviewed by TCM’s Ben Mankiewicz, as well as writer/director David O. Russell in conversation with Career Producer honoree Todd Black about their upcoming sports film “Madden,” Aaron Sorkin opining about “The Social Reckoning,” and a talk with “The Odyssey” production designer Ruth De Jong, a Charlottesville native.

Related Stories
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon to Present Free ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ New York City Screenings
Sandra Hüller’s Star Keeps Rising, but She’s Still Adjusting to Life in the Public Eye

On the first go-round, it’s fun to navigate new towns (downtown Charlottesville is walkable and charming), tourist attractions (I have not yet checked out Monticello), and complex ticketing systems. The press corps at this festival is slightly less awards-focused than Middleburg (Vanity Fair, Filmmaker Magazine, Vulture, RogerEbert.com, THR, and The Daily Beast among them). The price of an airplane ticket, hotel room, and access to screenings and talent brings with it the job of introducing movies (in my case, French Oscar entry “Minotaur”) and moderating Q&As (I’m talking to “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” writer/director Tim Blake Nelson). And my “Screen Talk” co-host Ryan Lattanzio and I are welcoming a special guest to a live podcast, “Paper Tiger” director James Gray.

Opening night, the festival showcased Julianne Moore’s Oscar frontrunner performance in “The Debut,” which just won Middleburg’s audience award and played just as well for the enthusiastic crowds at the Paramount Theatre, followed by an opening night gala attended by Ilya Tovbis, the festival’s artistic director, and Jody Kielbasa, UVA Vice Provost for the Arts and VAFF Executive Director. “The Debut” also opened well at Woodstock in Upstate New York last week, where Ryan attended and hosted a talk with “The Liberation” star Carrie Coon and writer/director Guy Nattiv.

The VAFF lineup is chock full of the usual awards suspects, from “La Bola Negra” and “Behemoth!” and “Being Heumann” to “14th,” “Club Kid,” “Wild Horse Nine,” and “Elsinore.”

entry.title: Sandra Hüller’s Star Keeps Rising, but She’s Still Adjusting to Life in the Public Eye
entry.summary: The Telluride Tributee breaks down a massive year that includes "Fatherland," "Rose," "Project Hail Mary," and "Digger."
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. MUBI opens “Fatherland” in select theaters starting Friday, October 23.]

After two Telluride Film Festival tributes, Sandra Hüller left the mountains to return to her hometown of Leipzig, Germany, where she is raising a 15-year-old daughter and directing a play. She’s still adjusting to her global rising star status. She’s directing because she has given up on theater acting.

The comedy “Toni Erdmann” put her on the map in 2016, followed by her Oscar-nominated role as a woman accused of killing her husband in Justine Triet’s “Anatomy of a Fall” (2023). She also earned raves as a bovine Nazi wife in “The Zone of Interest” that year.

Related Stories
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon to Present Free ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ New York City Screenings
‘Blue Film’: How the Controversial Camboy Drama Was Produced for Just $100,000

In 2026, she took on four movies, two black-and-white European projects and two big-budget Hollywood blockbusters. She won the Berlinale Silver Bear for her performance as a 17th-century war veteran living as a man in Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose” (MUBI), followed by her first studio gig as Eva Stratt, the scientist assigned to save the world in blockbuster “Project Hail Mary” (Amazon/MGM). And she returned to Cannes in Pawel Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” (MUBI) as Erika Mann, the car-driver daughter of Nobel Prize-winning novelist Thomas Mann.

“Fatherland” offers a mere slice of the scion Erika Mann, wealthy, privileged, educated, who could warrant a film of her own. The fact that she was married to the gay British poet W.H. Auden is a throwaway in the film, in which she serves as her elderly father’s assistant and representative on a 1949 post-war road trip back to East and West Germany. She’s in charge.

“She’s a race car driver, amongst other things,” said Hüller over coffee. “She’s also an author, journalist, an actor. Pawel wanted her to be a part of this journey because, in reality, she wasn’t. It was somebody else in the car. He wanted her to be the person responsible.”

The Buick was a monster. “It’s really heavy,” said Hüller. “It takes some effort to drive it. Because we don’t have help with the steering wheel. It takes some muscle.” That’s what sets the German actress apart from the field. She’s tall, lithe, intelligent, androgynous, vulnerable, and powerful all at once.

“Fatherland” kicks off with a bravura five-and-a-half minute locked-off single take of Klaus (August Diehl) in Cannes, sitting naked on the floor by a bed with a sleeping young man. He talks on the phone with Erika, who tries to coax her depressed drug-addict intellectual twin to come on a road trip with her back to Germany as his father accepts the Goethe prize. Hüller had long wanted to work with Diehl but had to settle for a phone call from her kitchen. (They will work together on another German film, about the painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and his partner Erna Schilling.)

Central to the journey is the dynamic between the father and the daughter, because she’s really angry with him. “When I read their letters to each other,” said Hüller, “they were what we say schonungslos. They didn’t spare each other from criticism. They were open, but they were forgiving each other at the same time. It was a deep, respectful love that they had, and a beautiful relationship. They are in a big conflict with each other at that point of their lives, and it’s painful because they love each other so much. When this loved person is dying, and they don’t agree on how to deal with it, that is devastating.”

According to Hüller, many German films have tried to portray the Manns, “but it’s a complicated family structure,” she said, “and also a complicated moral question around them. They left Germany during the war because it was too dangerous, and as we can see in the film, some people still didn’t forgive them. So it’s a discussion: What would you do if you were privileged? Would you use this privilege, or would you say, ‘I don’t care, I’ll stay here and watch everybody die.’ It’s a big topic.”

Erika Mann’s own homosexual relationships are only slightly referenced. “The person that she meets, this other journalist,” said Hüller, “she’s been in a relationship with her before, and they broke up for I can’t remember the reason. That’s also part of her freedom: not to talk about who she is and what she prefers, and I admire that.”

In one party scene in a night club Mann has a memorable face-off with her ex-husband Gustaf Gründgens, an actor who stayed behind and collaborated with the Nazis. “We always try to imagine ourselves as these superior creatures that do everything right,” said Hüller, “but we actually don’t know what we would do in a situation like this. Joachim Meyerhoff who was playing Gründgens, is an idol for me in German theater. He’s somebody whom we all know, and it was a great choice to let him play this person. I felt honored that I was allowed to slap him in the face, if you know what I mean.”

“Rose” is a less expressive role. No temper tantrums allowed. Blending into a strict rural community required discipline and rigor. When does this woman disguised as a man pee? How does she satisfy her wife? (She acquired dildos during her decade as a soldier in the 30 Years War.) As constrained as the character is, the actress shows us what she is feeling. “This is kind of a defect,” said Hüller. “I can’t hide what I feel. Like never, which is sometimes difficult in life. Even if I wanted to. But in this case, I felt like her whole existence after she chose to live in men’s clothes and to have the identity of a man to the outside, I don’t even know what her inner identity is. She has to be so aware of everything around her that she’s more a spectator of everything than an active subject.”

Survival was key. “She has to have a 360 degrees view of everything all the time,” said Hüller, “because she should never come into a situation where she has to act in a rush or where she would use gestures that are not appropriate for her chosen character. So it had to be contained. She’s coming from a long war. There’s a lot of damage and grief and darkness inside that person. And what I love about her the most is that she’s able to transform it into something soft, in a way. I loved her for not becoming this harsh, hard, cynical person.”

Next up the actress is taking on the portrayal of a man, German artist Wolfgang Herrndorf, in Maria Schrader’s “Work And Structure.” “It’s different because he’s not hiding anything,” said Hüller. “He’s just Wolfgang Herrndorf. I’m playing a man, but not trying to play a man. I look androgynous. I was born this way, and sometimes I can profit from it, not always, but sometimes.”

For her first studio gig, she took on powerful project director Eva Stratt in “Project Hail Mary,” assigned to save the world. After Hüller met Phil Lord and Chris Miller in London, she felt she could work with them. “I had no idea how to play her,” she said. “I was thinking about somebody completely different who could inhabit this strength and responsibility and clarity. But there are moments when other people think you can do it. You start to think you can do it yourself. But I would never have thought that somebody would think of me in a character like that.”

While she had to make some adjustments to working on a big-budget Hollywood movie, “I was surprised that there was so much freedom,” she said. “I would have expected it to be much more formal and more delivery oriented, but it wasn’t. And it had a lot to do with the people who were working on this because Chris and Phil are playful and open directors, and they give a lot of space to explore things. And Ryan [Gosling] is somebody who loves that too. So I never felt pressed into something that I don’t belong in. I was lucky.”

While the new idea of Stratt singing karaoke at a party threw her at first, Hüller came around. It happened because Gosling heard her singing on set. She loves to sing. “It’s annoying for people around me,” she said. “My daughter is always rolling her eyes. At first I thought, ‘why would she? it’s not her thing. It’s not her position to do that.’ But then I thought, ‘yeah, maybe that’s interesting that she’s leaving that position for that particular moment.'”

Hüller searched the libraries of goodbye songs. And producer Amy Pascal suggested a few songs that she was sure she could clear. “The next night, I found [Harry Styles’ song “Sign of the Times”] and sent it to her and asked if she could she could make this possible and she did. And the next day we shot it.”

The upcoming “Digger” (Legendary/Warner Bros.) is another big studio project, where Hüller plays the half-sister of Tom Cruise for one of her favorite directors, A.G. Iñárritu. “He’s very energetic,” she said. “He’s leading this whole shooting day in a way that you want to keep up with him. It’s inspiring to see him and his energy and his commitment to what he’s doing, and he’s sharing thoughts about everything. He’s trying things. Sometimes we do things completely different on another day. So he’s looking for the best thing that can happen.”

She enjoyed working with the “focused” Cruise, but did not hang out with him. “I felt like these two chose each other, the director and the actor. They really wanted to do this together. That was great to watch.”

The actress made the transition to directing at her Leipzig theater group last year. “I’m part of a theater collective of people who have known each other also for 20, 30 years,” she said. “Because the reception of my appearance on stage has changed a little bit through this public eye, I didn’t feel safe on stage anymore. The decision to go to the other side was a good decision because there’s so much to learn, and I enjoy it. I might go back. But I took some time to adjust my expectations. I went to the theater to be part of a group, but when you’re in this exhibited position, I didn’t know how to deal with that, and maybe I’ll be ready in the coming years to own that different position that I have. But I was a bit heartbroken that I lost it.”

One aspect of stardom that Hüller has embraced is red carpet fashion. “I have a team with Jordan Johnson Chung, who is choosing the outfits for me,” she said. “And I’m lucky to work with Chanel and people who help me with hair and makeup. But for me, in my life, I like to get up and get out of the house without anything. It’s always a bit of an adjustment to make. But when we do it, it’s fun.”

The promo tour for “Digger” will pull her back in. And the award season beckons. “It’s a challenge to find the balance between your personal life and decisions,” she said. “I don’t have a team around me when I’m at home. I have things to do. But I also want to help the films wherever I can. So I have to try and find the balance between. All of these things come with responsibility. It’s hard for me to to step away from that, like when a studio says, ‘But it’s your responsibility to be at that press day.’ No, it’s not.”

The actress is picky about her projects and has turned many things down, she said: “Not enough, some people think. I roll my eyes when I have to bring emotional value to a project that doesn’t genuinely have it. So if a script isn’t good, but I’m asked to make it good with acting, that’s something that I’m not here for. I don’t like that.”

entry.title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon to Present Free ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ New York City Screenings
entry.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon will present free screenings of 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem' in New York City on October 24 and 25.
entry.content:
The Greaves family‘s “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” is making waves in this year’s Best Documentary Feature Oscar race — and it’s about to screen for free throughout New York City this weekend.

A day after Neon announced a partnership with The Guardian to expand the theatrical release of another documentary Oscar contender, “NAZA,” the company is now partnering with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to bring “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” to more audiences.

Four free screenings of the film, co-directed by the late William Greaves with his son David, will roll out on Saturday, October 24, and Sunday, October 25, in New York City. The screenings will take place at the AMC Magic Johnson Harlem, Film Forum, and Film at Lincoln Center, “celebrating the legacy of the Harlem Renaissance and the enduring global power of art, culture, and creativity,” per the announcement.

Related Stories
‘Blue Film’: How the Controversial Camboy Drama Was Produced for Just $100,000
‘A Talent for Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich Face Off in This Punchy Twist on Patricia Highsmith

“’Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ brings the personalities, ideas, and debates behind the Harlem Renaissance to life for a new generation of New Yorkers,” Mamdani said in a statement. “We are proud to partner with the filmmaking team to offer free screenings to New Yorkers this weekend, ensuring that as many New Yorkers as possible get the chance to experience this film. Our city owes a debt of gratitude to the artists of the Harlem Renaissance whose enduring legacy is still felt in every jazz club, in every gallery, and in the movement for social justice that still continues to this day.”

The film premiered at Sundance before moving on to play Cannes, Telluride, Toronto, and New York, among other festivals. Nominated for five Critics Choice Documentary Awards, the film compiles footage William Greaves shot in 1972 of a gathering of Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington’s townhouse. William’s granddaughter, Liani Greaves, produced the film, with her father David co-directing. Before the younger Greaves took on the project, William’s wife, Louise Archambault, worked tirelessly to bring it to life after William died in 2014. Louise died in 2023.

“William Greaves believed deeply in the power of art to preserve history as well as inspire audiences and future generations. We know it would have meant so much to him to see Mayor Mamdani and the Office of the Mayor champion this film and help bring it to New Yorkers and especially back to Harlem where he was born and raised,” said David and Liani Greaves.

entry.title: ‘Blue Film’: How the Controversial Camboy Drama Was Produced for Just $100,000
entry.summary: How 'Blue Film,' the story of a camboy and his pedophile client, was produced for a mere $100,000.
entry.content:
The cast and crew of “Blue Film” were popping the champagne when disaster struck. The microbudget drama had just wrapped its final shot, managing to complete the controversial story of a cam boy and his pedophile client in 11 days and for just $45,000. That’s when Bijan Kazerooni, one of the film‘s producers, was called over to talk to cinematographer Ryan Jackson-Healy in his car.

“He is sitting there white-knuckling the steering wheel, and he goes, ‘We lost the day,'” Kazerooni remembered.

The production’s hard drive had failed, meaning they lost all the footage they had shot that day, including a wrenching monologue performed by Reed Birney, the film’s star. After taking a breath, Kazerooni cobbled together an additional day of photography.

Related Stories
‘A Talent for Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich Face Off in This Punchy Twist on Patricia Highsmith
Is Fan Fiction Really the Next Frontier in IP?

“We had to call everybody back for that 12th day, and because it’s last minute, not all of our crew was available, so we had to find new people, and we had to extend the actors’ hotels for a day, and change the flights,” Kazerooni said. “That’s the thing that really kicks your ass on these tiny budgets, because I can negotiate with a camera shop about pricing all day long. I can’t negotiate with Delta Airlines.”

In the end, the filmmakers shot “Blue Film” for $50,000 and spent an additional $50,000 on post-production. Much of the money came from indie maverick Mark Duplass, who challenged the producers and writer/director Elliott Tuttle to make a film on that shoestring budget.

“You can’t do half a day on production on a union shoot for $50,000,” Kazerooni said. “You can’t make a short film for $50,000 anymore. I’ve produced short films since ‘Blue Film’ that have cost more than our entire production budget.”

“Blue Film” hit that target because Tuttle purposely designed the movie to be as cost-efficient as possible. There are just two characters: Birney, who plays a john with a dark secret, and Kieron Moore, who stars as a fetish camboy who agrees to spend the night. Most of the film, meanwhile, was shot in one location: a Hancock Park house owned by the friend of producer Waylon Sall. It cost the production $1,000 to rent for the month.

“They had just moved out of their home, and the new tenant hadn’t moved in yet, so I was able to get a favorable deal,” Sall said. “We shot there for pennies and were able to dress it like a vacant Hollywood Airbnb.”

The actors worked for scale, which also kept costs to a minimum. But the production made a point of putting backend participation into contracts. Of course, assembling the cast had its challenges. Birney, a Tony Award winner with memorable turns on screen in “Mass” and “The Menu,” knew Adam Kersh, a producer and manager with indie ties. But finding the right actor to play Aaron Eagle, the sex worker who captivates Birney’s character, took some maneuvering.

“It was harder to attach a casting director because of the content of the movie than it was to attach Reed,” Kersh said. “We had a lot of passes. They were all afraid of it.”

Fortunately, Eleonore Hendricks, whose credits include “Stand Clear of the Closing Doors,” signed on, which helped legitimize the production. She discovered Moore, an English actor who appeared in “Boots” and “Vampire Academy.”

“Blue Film” also benefited from other experienced hands, including Jackson-Healy, who served as cinematographer on “Mass,” and editor Zach Clark (“Our Son”). It also benefited from several volunteer PAs.

“My housemates would come with me at two a.m. to load out and load in,” admits Kazerooni.

Though Birney and Moore were used to more creature comforts, they embraced the micro-budget atmosphere.

“Both of our talent are nonlocal, so flying them out and putting them up for a little over 20 days, from a budget standpoint, was awful,” Kazerooni said. “But they were very patient with me when I called them and proposed certain flights that were maybe not the class they would have wanted. What made everything possible was a willingness from our cast and from our crew to tolerate indie film conditions and to not balk at things.”

And the actors were willing to suffer for their art. Moore, for instance, spends the second half of the film shirtless after allowing Birney’s character to shave his chest.

“We had to shoot everything with him with hair, then get the hair off,” Sall said. “Kieron didn’t want to be shaved. He wanted to get waxed. So, we have one night before a two-day break. We finish shooting and call a waxing place to stay open late for us, so we can take Kieron straight from set to the salon. Kieron had a lot of hair. He’s British. He’s pale. He was in a lot of pain. He pushed himself to the limit. I was there with him. He was screaming that he wanted to kill me, but you know the results are undeniable. It gave him a natural, razor-burn look. I wish there were a less painful alternative, but it worked.”

Kersh is a veteran who produced the indie hit “Between the Temples,” but the rest of the production team was relatively new to features.

“We were all figuring out how to make a tiny, tiny movie together,” said Will Youmans, one of the producers. “But it was great to find a group of people who wanted to do something together and who just decided to make it happen.”

Tuttle acknowledges the film was a no-frills affair, but credits the producers with letting him focus on putting the story on screen without getting consumed by the cost of everything.

“I was never worried about anything production-wise — not once,” Tuttle said. “It seems insane to think about making a movie for that number in that amount of days. But because of my team, I didn’t have to think about the logistical nightmare of making an indie film. I just got to be creatively fulfilled.”

However, even after the film came in on budget, finding a distributor for the hot-button project wasn’t easy. Sundance, SXSW, and other major festivals all passed after screening the movie. Finally, the Edinburgh Festival stepped up and accepted the film. That’s when critics embraced the picture, raising its profile.

“Premiering in Scotland changed everything,” Kersh said.

Eventually, Obscured Releasing, a newcomer to the distribution scene, bought the film’s U.S. rights and released it in theaters last summer. It earned $144,371 in limited release and found a wider audience when it premiered on demand. Kersh says the film is poised to recoup its initial investment and distribution expenses. It is expected to turn a profit. “Blue Film” has also secured distribution in international markets, including the U.K., Germany, and Latin America. Despite some setbacks, the producers believe that the film is more successful than a film about a camboy and a pedophile could have ever hoped to be.

“I get lots of calls from people being like, ‘How do I get money for my film? How do I pull off something like this?'” said Youmans. “And the answer is like, you get money for your movie the way you get money for anything in your life, which is any way you can. There’s no magic to it.”

entry.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3 Review: Netflix’s Fizzy Rom-Com Puts the Pop (and Pain) Back Into Modern Love
entry.summary: Long-billed as the series' "champagne" season, the Adam Brody- and Kristen Bell-starring comedy goes down easy. Well, mostly.
entry.content:
There’s nothing quite like a good theme. (See: a Christmas-centric episode late in the third season of Netflix‘s darling rom-com, “Nobody Wants This.”) Before the Erin Foster-created series rolled out its latest 10 episodes, the show’s team was firmly aligned behind an overall concept: This is the champagne season. It’s bubbly and fun! Celebratory and bright! And while that is mostly true — especially as it applies to the romance of our leads Joanne (Kristen Bell) and Noah (Adam Brody) — there’s another, darker theme lurking just underneath.

Self-sabotage.

So, no, not nearly as bubbly or bright. And yet, after a disappointing second season that trafficked in flimsy retread (beyond this critic’s favorite subplot, which we will return to soon), a hearty dose of “well, that’s real life for ya” is welcome. So, too, is the champagne of it all.

Related Stories
‘A Talent for Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich Face Off in This Punchy Twist on Patricia Highsmith
Is Fan Fiction Really the Next Frontier in IP?

First things first, after two seasons of (light, destined to be cleared up) back-and-forth, Joanne and Noah have moved in together. “We live together” the duo dreamily and repeatedly huff at each other in the premiere, and thank goodness they’re so damn cute, because that would wear thin with any other couple. (Another treat: their gorgeous new home, which seems to have been dropped, fully formed and decorated, right into their laps.)

Elsewhere, housing is a real problem. Sasha (Timothy Simons) and Esther (Jackie Tohn) have agreed to try the “nesting” approach to their separation, with each of them switching out of the family home, all the better to leave their daughter, Miriam (Shiloh Bearman), feeling secure in their love. Morgan (Justine Lupe), meanwhile, has moved back in with her and Joanne’s mother, Lynn (Stephanie Faracy), who is just delighted when Sasha starts spending his non-nesting time there, too.

Alas! Joanne and Noah’s domestic bliss is not quite what it seems, as they struggle to marry their different approaches (to morning routines, to cleaning, etc.). Also a problem: their new neighbor, Travis (Avan Jogia), who is revealed to be Joanne’s ex, and whose reappearance in her life almost immediately reactivates lots of old wounds. (This particular subplot mostly rankles, at least until that second-half Christmas episode, which adds in some very necessary flashbacks and context.)

Old wounds are Joanne’s speciality, and they’re really activated by her conversion work. Rabbi Eden (a wonderfully low-key Sarah Silverman) might be open to Joanne’s foray into Judaism, but the rest of her conversion class isn’t sold on her and her “drama” (especially Andrew Rannells, who is on hand mostly to, well, be Andrew Rannells). Even worse? As Joanne’s self-regard takes a hit, Noah’s inflates, especially when it becomes clear to him that he might have a place at his old temple after all. (Consider his Season 2 work subplot officially non-essential.)

And while Joanne is busy with all these parts of her new life, Morgan finds her own professional horizons also increasing. Once linked and bonded by their podcast, Morgan goes viral during a one-off episode (co-starring, of all people, Sasha) in which she somewhat accidentally creates her own, deeply Morgan-esque life philosophy: “Make them.” Screw “let them”! Morgan is going to turn this whole thing into her own cottage industry, even if it requires her to write a book (?) which is, to put it kindly, not where her skills lie, even if a proposed chapter on “lip glosses that are too sticky” sounds like a banger. (Esther also takes on a new gig as a realtor, while Sasha uses “make them” on his own father to startling effect.)

Ah, Sasha and Morgan. While the series has been up and down and back and forth on the bond (fine, I’ll say it, the flirtation) between the second-class siblings, Season 3 finally addresses their spark head-on. And self-sabotage? Yes, that’s indeed on the menu. While Sasha attempts to get back into the dating pool — the shock that Esther is also on the apps is one of the great eye-poppers of the season — he can’t fight that the one person he most wants to spend time with is Morgan. And as the Roklov and Williams families grow still more entangled, the possibility of their own match feels, if not inevitable, at least on the table.

No, no, no, I understand this concept might be a non-starter for many fans. For awhile there, it was even a non-starter for the show, which faced backlash for Season 1’s treatment of it and wildly course-corrected in Season 2. And even for this critic, who remains truly devoted to Esther and Sasha, talking about this development in a positive fashion just feels wrong.

But life (and love) are messy, an idea that “Nobody Wants This” is re-embracing, even as its central couple grows closer than ever. Joanne and Noah’s happily-ever-after feels more secure than ever this season — what a concept! — but that means some of the usual drama needs to be shifted to other love stories. Morgan and Sasha are the right place for it. Champagne? Maybe not, but as much pleasure as a settled Joanne and Noah bring, a flirty and lightly terrified Sasha and Morgan add some real fizz.

Season 3 includes a number of episodes with one-off settings or situations: a dizzy housewarming party that brings everyone together, a sweaty heatwave that turns into a raucous pool party, a fake-out wedding that helps clarify for Joanne just how good she’s got it right now (with a twist we won’t spoil here, it’s just too darling to unveil), but it’s Episode 7 that most stands out. That’s the one that pulls Sasha and Morgan out of their comfort zone (and literal time zone), removes Joanne and Noah from the picture (it’s the sabbath, so they can’t be on their phones), and makes a choice about their relationship that no one can take back.

What follows is not just self-sabotage, but the crackling possibility of real self-reinvention, something both Joanne and Noah have already embraced. But that kind of growth opportunity is not only hard-won, but just plain hard. Is Sasha the love of Morgan’s life? Or is he just in her life to teach her what it really feels like to be loved? “Nobody Wants This” has asked this question before. It will probably ask this question again. But it’s meaningful, gorgeous query to ponder. Now, can everyone get out of their own way, and keep up that kind of deep-thinking momentum into Season 4 and beyond?

No more sabotage. It’s time to take a drink of what life is really offering you. Careful, it’s fizzy.

Grade: B+

“Nobody Wants This” Season 3 premiered Thursday, October 22 on Netflix. All 10 episodes were released at once.

entry.title: ‘A Talent for Murder’ Review: Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich Face Off in This Punchy Twist on Patricia Highsmith
entry.summary: TIFF: Anton Corbijn directs Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich in 'A Talent for Murder,' a two-hander with real bite. Review.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 14, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.]

In recent years, movie audiences have fallen back in love with the whodunnit, thanks to the mighty talents of Rian Johnson and Kenneth Branagh and more. That the classic mystery subgenre would continue to stake its claim in the cinematic world is no surprise. When executed well, there’s nothing quite so fun as going for a ride that ends with a tidy, smart ending. This is who did the deed, and this is how they did it, and this is why.

Related Stories
Is Fan Fiction Really the Next Frontier in IP?
When VFX and Practical Sets Work Together, Sometimes You Invent New Cameras

Iconic novelist Patricia Highsmith was far more concerned with the final part of that particular answer. Why. The creator of Tom Ripley wasn’t very interested in untangling who — we always knew who! — but what made him (or her other, often less popular creations) tick. Whydunnit, as it were. And Highsmith’s own compulsion toward building twisted, twisty characters is given fresh life (new blood?) in Anton Corbijn’s clever “A Talent for Murder,” adapted by playwright Joanna Murray-Smith, who first constructed this slice of fiction for her play “Switzerland.”

Built on the barest of real facts — like that Highsmith was a prickly customer who spent her final years basically holed up in a Swiss home that people called “the bunker” — Murray-Smith spins out her own story of psychological trauma and maybe, just maybe, actual murder. Starring a wonderfully terrifying Dame Helen Mirren as this fictionalized Highsmith, the film opens with a clearly out-of-his-depth (or is he?) young editor making his way to the bunker in question. To the prickly customer in question.

Edward Ridgeway (Alden Ehrenreich) is, in fact, the young second editor dispatched to Switzerland to try to extract a final Ripley novel from Highsmith (the film was shot on location, and it shows). The first one, well, we’ll hear a bit more about him along the way, but suffice to say, their meeting didn’t end so well. Highsmith’s publisher is intent on getting one more Ripley hit out of the author, and if Edward can’t get her to sign a new contract? He might as well not come back. Slightly disheveled, a little shy, and obviously out of place, it’s safe to assume Edward might not be the guy for the job.

Highsmith (Mirren’s portrayal of the author, fictional as it might be, is still so mighty it feels wrong to call her Patricia, but we will try) feels the same way. Still, it’s hard to imagine who could possibly impress Patricia, as she rattles around her bunker (impeccably designed by Dimitri Capuani), smokes a lot, and grimaces frequently at her typewriter. That’s not to say that Patricia doesn’t know Edward, or expect him, or see through him. Mirren’s Patricia intermittently narrates the story, suggesting she’s creating Edward as much as she is receiving him. Why not both?

But Edward’s nerdy charm isn’t without some admirers, like alluring young Clementine (Olivia Cooke), who he meets on the train to Switzerland. (Yes, many Highsmith faithful will undoubtedly point at the screen when they first come into contact, all the better to point out these “strangers on a train.”) They meet cute and then meet again (and again), giving Ehrenreich space to build an impressively multifaceted character who seems to adjust to whomever he’s dealing with.

But the scenes of Edward and Patricia together? They’re the best, and the film is at its strongest when these two are going at it, trying to catch each other out, spinning tales to entertain and scare, and testing for weak spots. Patricia’s home is kitted out with all manner of deadly items: poisons line her pantry, knives and guns adorn her office wall, and there has to be something wrong with her aquarium filled with snails. But Edward, possessed of a tragic backstory and an iron will, isn’t giving up so easily. He’ll buy her a knife. He’ll eat a breakfast made next to a bottle of poison. He’ll get the girl.

Perhaps Patricia has misjudged him? Or have we?

Corbijn delights in showing us what to look at — Edward’s bag, for instance, or a ranting man in the airport, a knife or two, Clementine’s luggage tag — and then making us look again, with fresh eyes. As Edward chips away at Patricia’s resistance, the pair start to build a new story for Ripley, together. And as they do, we get to watch that same story play out on screen, with Ehrenreich ably slipping into the Ripley role, Cooke recast as his mark. It’s not just a wily way to unspool a new, meta mystery. It also offers Ehrenreich to really show off his stuff, running away with the film by way of his many ever-shifting characters.

While Murray-Smith’s script keeps a steady head on the multiplying storylines — Edward and Patricia at work, Edward and Clementine at play, Tom and “Clementine” delighting across Rome — the film does lose some steam when it veers too far off the two-hander nature that powered its first half. Watching Ehrenreich slip into Tom Ripley’s skin is a hoot, but it’s more edifying watching him face off against Mirren. The film offers no neat answers to its many characters and plotlines, but perhaps that’s the real joy of the mystery: actual mystery, and an enduring obsession with how this all fits together. Maybe it doesn’t, but it’s sure fun to watch.

Grade: B

“A Talent for Murder” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.
